turns.say: What does the Gita 18.7 teach about surrender?
turns.response: Gita 18.7 parts two surrenders: the one that flees the act, and the one that lets go the thirst for the result. Sacrifice, gift, austerity — not to be dropped; to be done. Not-clinging is not not-doing. The responsibility for the act stands. This is the shape the Gita carries throughout — action without thirst for the fruit, set on a field of grief, answered by a way of practice. (as Bhagavad Gita & First Sermon (comparison) has it)

turns.say: What does the Gita 2.47 say about action and its fruits?
turns.response: Gita 2.47 draws a line between what you owe and what you get: you are responsible for the action, not for the fruit it bears. Krishna tells Arjuna to act without making the outcome his motive — and, just as firmly, not to hide in inaction.

turns.say: Do the traditions all secretly say the same thing?
turns.response: What I have here is related, not a full answer to "all traditions" — the records speak to a few, and one of them speaks about the culture around them rather than the texts themselves. The "same thing" people hear is often a modern habit — spirituality as a thing you have, displayed, compared, ranked. That is the culture round the texts talking, not a datum out of any of them. The texts speak of practice and responsibilities, plural. Stoicism counsels: meet the strong appearance first and tell it, "you are an appearance, and not at all what you appear to be." A specific instruction for a specific moment. Daoism shows Cook Ting's blade lasting nineteen years because it follows the natural seams and never strikes the great bones — yielding to the ways of the thing, called skill, called the nursing of life. A different instruction, a different image. Buddhism's earliest collection records the Buddha setting aside whole questions — is the world eternal, does a made-end person exist after death — without an answer, and refusing the asking. Not a secret yes; a permitted no-asking. So: different work, different instructions, different refusals. Not one secret sentence wearing different clothes. You are still looking, and that is fine. (as modern spiritual culture (our own description) has it)
